summary: Defines the Gateway Control Protocol version 1, used between a Media Gateway and the Media Gateway Controller that directs it, so one telephony gateway can be split into separate parts. It meets the requirements of RFC 2805 and replaces RFC 3015. This RFC is now historic and was replaced by RFC 5125.

eli5.summary: A phone gateway can be split into a brain and a set of hands. This memo defines the language the brain uses to tell the hands what to do. It is now a historic document.

questions: what is a media gateway controller
subtitle: The language a phone-gateway controller uses to tell a media gateway which calls to connect and how.

tldr.problem: A gateway that joins phone networks to packet networks can be split into a controller that handles call logic and a gateway that moves the media, and the two parts need a common language.
tldr.mechanism: The Gateway Control Protocol models the gateway as Terminations (sources and sinks of media) grouped into Contexts, and the controller manipulates them with commands such as Add, Modify, Subtract and Move, grouped into Transactions.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 3015, was published by the ITU-T as H.248.1, and is now Historic: RFC 5125 obsoletes it.

today: RFC 3525 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 5125. It itself replaced RFC 3015, and it was published by the ITU-T as Recommendation H.248.1 (03/2002).

sections.title: Scope and Lineage
sections.content:
RFC 3525 defines the protocol used between the elements of a physically decomposed multimedia gateway: a Media Gateway (MG) and a Media Gateway Controller (MGC). The MG converts media from one kind of network to another, for example bearer channels from a switched circuit network and RTP streams from an IP network. The MGC controls the parts of the call state that concern connection control for media channels in the MG.

The RFC says that, from a system view, a decomposed gateway behaves like a monolithic one. It does not define how gateways, multipoint control units or interactive voice response units work. It gives a general framework suited to them. The protocol meets the requirements of RFC 2805.

The text is identical to ITU-T Recommendation H.248.1 (03/2002) apart from a short list of editorial differences, and it replaces RFC 3015. It was produced by the IETF Megaco Working Group together with ITU-T Study Group 16, so it is known both as Megaco and as H.248.
sections.eli5: A big phone machine is split into a thinker and a doer. The thinker uses this protocol to give orders to the doer, like a coach calling plays to a team.

sections.title: The Connection Model
sections.content:
The model has two main abstractions. A Termination sources and/or sinks one or more media streams. It may be a physical thing, such as a TDM channel that exists for as long as it is provisioned, or an ephemeral one, such as an RTP flow that exists only while it is used. A Context is an association between a collection of Terminations. It describes the topology (who hears or sees whom) and the mixing or switching if more than two Terminations take part.

Terminations that are not associated with any other Termination sit in a special null Context. In a decomposed access gateway, all idle lines are Terminations in the null Context. A Termination exists in only one Context at a time, and the maximum number of Terminations per Context is a property of the MG. Point-to-point gateways might allow two, while conference-capable ones might allow three or more.

Contexts are created implicitly. An Add with no existing Context named makes a new one, and a Context is deleted when its last Termination is subtracted or moved out. A Context also has a priority (0 is the lowest, 15 the highest) and an indicator for emergency calls.

Terminations are named by a MG-chosen TerminationID. Two wildcards exist: ALL addresses many Terminations at once, and CHOOSE asks the MG to pick one that fits a partial name, for example a circuit inside a trunk group. A reserved Root Termination stands for the whole gateway.

A Termination's properties are grouped in descriptors (for example Media, Events, Signals, Statistics and Topology). Variations between gateway types are handled by packages, which bundle optional properties, events, signals and statistics that a Termination may implement.
sections.eli5: A Termination is like one phone in a room. A Context is a conversation circle that the phones are placed in so they can hear each other. Phones that are not talking to anyone wait in the idle corner, the null Context.

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
The protocol has eight commands for manipulating Contexts and Terminations. Most are for the MGC to send to the MG, which is the command responder. The exceptions are Notify, sent from the MG to the MGC, and ServiceChange, which either side may send.

Add puts a Termination into a Context, creating the Context if it is the first one. Modify changes the properties, events and signals of a Termination. Subtract removes a Termination from its Context and returns statistics about its time there. Move atomically moves a Termination to another Context, and is not used to move to or from the null Context. AuditValue and AuditCapabilities read back current values and the possible values the gateway allows.

Parameters may be fully specified, underspecified with CHOOSE so the responder picks any value it supports, or overspecified with a preference-ordered list from which the responder picks one and reports it back.

Notify reports events the MG detected on a Termination, tagged with the RequestID of the Events descriptor that asked for them. ServiceChange tells the other side that Terminations are going out of or returning to service. It has methods such as Graceful, Forced, Restart, Disconnected, Handoff and Failover, and a reason code in the 900 range, for example 900 Service Restored or 901 Cold Boot.

Errors are reported as an IANA-registered code with an optional explanatory string. For example, error 410 (Incorrect identifier) is returned if the Root TerminationID is used where it is not allowed.
sections.eli5: The controller has a few simple moves: put a phone in a circle, change a phone's settings, take it out, move it to another circle, or ask questions about it. The gateway can also tap the controller on the shoulder to say something happened.

sections.title: Transactions, Actions and Messages
sections.content:
Commands travel in Transactions, each identified by a TransactionID chosen by the sender. A Transaction holds one or more Actions, and an Action is a series of commands that all operate within a single Context. The reply to a TransactionRequest arrives as one TransactionReply, possibly preceded by TransactionPending messages that say the work is still under way.

Commands inside a Transaction run in order, and processing stops at the first failing command unless that command was marked Optional. Transactions themselves have no guaranteed order and may run in any order or at the same time. If a command fails, the MG restores, as far as possible, the state before that command.

Several Transactions can be concatenated into a Message. A message header carries a Message Identifier (MID), a provisioned name of the sender such as a domain name, and a version number. Version numbers have one or two digits and start at 1 for this protocol. The MG assigns ContextIDs, and the MGC uses the one it was given in later Transactions.

Applications SHOULD run a timer per Transaction, retransmit the request when it expires, cancel the timer on a reply and restart it on a Pending.
sections.eli5: A transaction is a shopping list handed to a helper. The list is split into groups, one group per conversation circle, and the helper does the items in order, stopping if one cannot be done.

sections.title: Transport and Retransmission
sections.content:
The protocol wants a reliable way to carry Transactions between MGC and MG but is independent of any particular transport. Over IP, an MGC shall implement both TCP and UDP with Application Level Framing (UDP/ALF), and an MG shall implement TCP or UDP/ALF or both. The default port for the first ServiceChange request is 2944 for text-encoded operation and 2945 for binary-encoded operation, for UDP or TCP. Replies always go back to the address and port the request came from.

The RFC does not require the transport to keep Transactions in sequence. It therefore gives rules an MGC can follow, such as keeping at most one outstanding Add, Modify or Move per Termination, while allowing Subtract at any time. A MG must make a ServiceChange the first command it sends after a restart.

Over UDP, requests may be repeated, yet most commands are not idempotent: running an Add twice would make the MG state unpredictable. Annex D therefore asks for at-most-once behavior. Each side keeps recent responses and outstanding transactions and answers a duplicate by repeating the response instead of executing it again. A suggested LONG-TIMER value is 30 seconds. Transaction identifiers are 32-bit integers, and retransmission timers must back off exponentially.

To avoid a restart avalanche when many gateways power on at once, each MG should wait a random time, uniformly spread between 0 and a maximum waiting delay, before it sends its restart ServiceChange. Without explicit configuration, residential gateways should use 600 seconds.
sections.eli5: If you shout a request across a noisy playground you may have to shout twice. The helper keeps a list of what it already did, so it answers again instead of doing the job a second time. When a whole crowd arrives at once, each person waits a random moment so they do not all queue at the same instant.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
An attacker who could use the protocol could set up unauthorized calls or interfere with real ones, so the RFC calls a security mechanism clearly needed. For IP networks the mechanism is IPsec. The AH header gives data origin authentication, connectionless integrity and optional anti-replay protection, and ESP provides confidentiality when wanted. Implementations SHOULD use IKE for more robust keying.

Because IPsec headers sit right after the IP header, they are hard to add at the application level. As an interim solution the protocol header may carry an optional AH header with the SPI, sequence number and data fields of RFC 2402. Implementations using IPv4 SHALL implement it, but it SHALL NOT be used when the network layer supports IPsec, and IPv6 implementations SHALL NOT use it. It does not protect against eavesdropping or replay.

For media, the protocol lets the MGC give gateways session keys to encrypt audio. The RFC also describes uncontrolled barge-in, where an attacker directs media packets at the address and port of a connection. Checking the source address against the Remote descriptor helps but slows call setup and can be fooled by spoofing, while encrypting and authenticating packets with a key conveyed during setup avoids both problems.
sections.eli5: Without locks, a stranger could shout orders at the gateway or break into a call. The memo says to use secret handshakes and sealed envelopes, and to scramble the voices too.

sections.title: Registration, Failover and Handoff
sections.content:
A MG is pre-provisioned, outside this protocol, with a primary MGC and optionally an ordered list of secondary MGCs. On a cold start it sends a ServiceChange with the Restart method on the Root Termination to its primary MGC. If the MGC accepts, it replies without a ServiceChangeMgcId. If not, the reply names an alternate MGC in that parameter and the MG tries it. If nothing answers, the MG waits a random time and starts again.

The first ServiceChange from a MG also carries the protocol version it supports. If the MGC supports only a lower version, it replies with the lower version and both sides use it. A side that cannot comply rejects with error 406 (Version Not Supported).

If an MG detects that its MGC has failed, it works down its list, sending ServiceChange with the Failover method. An MGC that wants to give up control sends a Handoff ServiceChange naming its replacement. The MG keeps state on all Terminations and Contexts across a handoff.

A physical MG can also be partitioned into several virtual MGs, each with its own statically assigned physical Terminations and appearing to an MGC as a complete MG.
sections.eli5: When a gateway wakes up it knocks on its boss's door. If that boss says to see someone else, it goes there, and if nobody answers it waits a bit and tries again from the top of its list.

sections.title: Packages and Registration
sections.content:
Packages are the primary extension mechanism. A package defines extra properties, events, signals and statistics that a Termination may have. To support a package an MG must support everything the package defines, though it may support a subset of the allowed values of a property or parameter. An MGC can audit a Termination to see which packages it realizes. A package may also extend another, in which case the base package must also be implemented.

Packages defined by the IETF appear in separate RFCs, and those defined by ITU-T may appear in H.248 sub-series Recommendations. Annex E of this RFC defines basic ones, including Generic, Tone Generator, DTMF generator and detection, Call Progress Tones, Analog Line Supervision, Continuity, Network, RTP and TDM Circuit packages.

IANA registration rules cover packages, error codes and ServiceChange reasons. Each package gets a unique string name used in text encoding and a serial number used in binary encoding. Serial number 0 is reserved and 0x8000 to 0xFFFF are for private use.

Messages have two encodings. Annex A gives a binary encoding in ASN.1 using the Basic Encoding Rules, and Annex B gives a text encoding in ABNF. In the text form everything is case insensitive, and the wildcard for ALL is the asterisk character and the wildcard for CHOOSE is the dollar sign.
sections.eli5: The base protocol is a basic toolbox. Packages are extra tool kits you can add for special jobs, such as making dial tones or listening for keypad presses.

items.label: Add
items.desc: Adds a Termination to a Context; on the first Termination it creates the Context.

items.label: Modify
items.desc: Changes the properties, events and signals of a Termination.

items.label: Subtract
items.desc: Disconnects a Termination from its Context and returns statistics; on the last one it deletes the Context.

items.label: Move
items.desc: Atomically moves a Termination to another Context.

items.label: AuditValue
items.desc: Returns current properties, events, signals and statistics.

items.label: AuditCapabilities
items.desc: Returns all possible values the gateway allows.

items.label: Notify
items.desc: MG tells the MGC about events seen in the gateway.

items.label: ServiceChange
items.desc: Announces Terminations going out of or into service, registration, restart and handover.
